title: Monitor and co-ordinate the harvesting of agricultural products

lessons.title: Preparing and co-ordinating the harvest
lessons.html:
The supervisor's role at harvest

Harvest is when the whole season's work turns into income. A supervisor co-ordinates people, equipment, transport and the packhouse or buyer so that the product is picked at the right time, at the right quality, and moved quickly.

Judging readiness

Harvest timing depends on maturity indicators set for the crop and the market, for example:

  • Colour charts for tomatoes, citrus or apples
  • Size or diameter rings for fruit and vegetables
  • Firmness (pressure tester) and sugar content (refractometer, measured as Brix)
  • Grain moisture content for maize, wheat and soybeans
  • Days after planting or flowering
  • Pre-harvest intervals for any sprays applied: check the spray records and labels; no harvest before the interval has passed

Planning the day

  • Which blocks or rows, in what order
  • Number of pickers and team leaders
  • Equipment: picking bags, crates, bins, ladders, secateurs, trailers, combine harvester
  • Transport to the packhouse, silo or market and expected collection times
  • Shade, water, toilets and handwashing facilities for workers

Briefing the team

Start each day with a short briefing: which block, what maturity and quality to pick, how to handle the product, safety rules and hygiene. Show examples of correct and rejected fruit. Clear instructions reduce rejections later.

Hygiene and food safety

  • Workers wash hands before work and after using the toilet.
  • No eating, smoking or spitting in the rows.
  • Sick workers, especially with diarrhoea or open wounds, report and do not handle produce.
  • Crates and bins are clean and never placed directly on soil where avoidable.

lessons.title: Monitoring harvest quality and output
lessons.html:
What to monitor during harvesting

  • Picking standard: correct maturity, size and no damaged fruit included.
  • Handling: fruit placed, not thrown; bags and crates not overfilled; no stems left that puncture other fruit; product kept out of the sun.
  • Losses: fruit left on plants or dropped on the ground; grain losses behind the combine.
  • Speed and flow: crates moving to collection points; no long waits in the heat.
  • Safety: safe ladder use, correct lifting, hydration and machinery rules.

Quality checks

Take random samples from crates or bins at collection points. Check for bruising, cuts, wrong size or colour, foreign objects and disease. Record the percentage of defects per team or picker. Give feedback immediately and correct problems.

Record keeping and traceability

Record for every load: date, block, crop and cultivar, number of crates or mass, team, and time dispatched. Use tickets or labels on bins. This allows the packhouse and buyers to trace product back to the block, which food safety schemes and customers require, and it supports payment of piece-work rates.

Post-harvest handling

  • Move product to shade or cold storage quickly; field heat speeds up deterioration.
  • Keep cold chain where required.
  • Separate rejected or damaged product.
  • For grain, check moisture before storage to avoid mould.

Machinery safety

With combines, tractors and trailers: only trained, authorised operators; keep people clear of moving parts and blind spots; switch off and remove the key before clearing blockages; no riders on trailers or drawbars.

End of day

Reconcile what was picked with what was delivered, clean equipment, report problems and plan the next day.

Key points

  • Use maturity indicators and check pre-harvest intervals before picking.
  • Plan people, equipment and transport for each day.
  • Brief teams on quality, handling, hygiene and safety.
  • Sample crates, record defects and give quick feedback.
  • Record every load for traceability and cool product fast.
